label: thm:thinall
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:thinall}
If $0<h/r\le1/4$, then
\[
 N_A\left(\Lambda\right)>\frac{D}{4}\Lambda
 \,\,\,\left(\Lambda\ge0\right),
 \,\,\,
 \nu_k\left(A_{r,r+h}\right)\le
 \frac{4k}{\left(r+h\right)^2-r^2}
 \,\,\,\left(k\ge1\right).
\]

label: cor:annularproducts
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:annularproducts}
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, be a bounded domain with
piecewise smooth boundary. The Neumann eigenvalues of
$A_{r,R}\times\Omega$, enumerated from $\mu_0=0$ and with
multiplicities, satisfy
\[
 \mu_k\left(A_{r,R}\times\Omega\right)\le
 4\pi^2\left(
 \frac{k}{\omega_{d+2}\left|A_{r,R}\right|\,\left|\Omega\right|}
 \right)^{2/\left(d+2\right)},\,\,\, k\ge1.
\]
In particular, every annular cylinder satisfies this inequality.
head: environment

label: cor:annularsectors
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:annularsectors}
For an integer $q\ge2$, let
\[
 S_q=\left\{
 \left(s\cos\theta,s\sin\theta\right):
 r<s<R,\ 0<\theta<2\pi/q
 \right\}.
\]
With Neumann conditions on the circular and straight parts of its
boundary, its counting function and eigenvalues satisfy
\[
 N_{S_q}\left(\Lambda\right)>\frac{\left|S_q\right|}{4\pi}\Lambda
 \,\,\,\left(\Lambda\ge0\right),\,\,\,
 \mu_k\left(S_q\right)\le\frac{4qk}{R^2-r^2}
 \,\,\,\left(k\ge1\right).
\]

label: lem:radial
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For every nonzero trial function,
\[
 \frac{\int_r^R m^2s^{-1}\left|u\right|^2\,\mathrm d s}
 {\int_r^R s\left|u\right|^2\,\mathrm d s}\le\frac{m^2}{r^2}.
\]
Adding this bound on the same trial subspace and applying the
min--max principle gives
$\lambda_{m,n}\le\lambda_{0,n}+m^2/r^2$.
Here $\lambda_{0,0}=0$. If $\lambda>0$ and
$-u''-s^{-1}u'=\lambda u$ with $u'\left(r\right)=u'\left(R\right)=0$, then $w=u'$
satisfies
\[
 -w''-s^{-1}w'+s^{-2}w=\lambda w,
 \,\,\, w\left(r\right)=w\left(R\right)=0.
\]
Conversely, for a nonzero solution of this Dirichlet problem, set
$u=-\left(w'+s^{-1}w\right)/\lambda$. The differential equation gives $u'=w$,
so $u$ solves the original Neumann problem. The maps are inverse.
Thus, including multiplicities, the positive radial Neumann spectrum
equals the Dirichlet spectrum in angular order one. The unitary
change $v=\sqrt{s}\,w$ turns the latter into
\[
 -v''+\frac{3}{4s^2}v=\lambda v,\,\,\, v\left(r\right)=v\left(R\right)=0.
\]
Comparison of its potential with $3/\left(4r^2\right)$ yields
$\lambda_{0,n}\le\left(\pi n/h\right)^2+3/\left(4r^2\right)$ for $n\ge1$.
The bound for $n=0$ follows separately from $\lambda_{0,0}=0$.

label: lem:sum
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $f\left(x\right)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ on $\left[0,1\right]$ and
$I=\int_0^1f\left(x\right)\,\mathrm d x=\pi/4$. For an integer $N\ge2$, let $U_1,\ldots,U_{N-1}$ be independent
uniform random variables on $\left[0,1\right]$, and let
$U_{\left(1\right)}\le\cdots\le U_{\left(N-1\right)}$ denote their
increasing rearrangement (the order statistics). For $1\le j\le N-1$, the density of
$U_{\left(j\right)}$ is
\[
 p_j\left(x\right)=
 \frac{\left(N-1\right)!}{\left(j-1\right)!\left(N-1-j\right)!}
 x^{j-1}\left(1-x\right)^{N-1-j},\qquad 0<x<1.
\]
Indeed, for small $\varepsilon>0$, one sample point falls in
$\left[x,x+\varepsilon\right]$, while exactly $j-1$ of the others
lie below $x$. Choosing these points gives the displayed coefficient
after dividing the probability by $\varepsilon$ and letting
$\varepsilon\to0+$. Events with two points in the short interval
have probability $O\left(\varepsilon^2\right)$ and do not affect the limit.
The elementary integral identity
\[
 \int_0^1x^p\left(1-x\right)^q\,\,\mathrm d x
 =\frac{p!q!}{\left(p+q+1\right)!},
 \qquad p,q\in\left\{0,1,\ldots\right\},
\]
obtained by repeated integration by parts, consequently gives
\[
 \mathbb E U_{\left(j\right)}
 =\int_0^1x p_j\left(x\right)\,\,\mathrm d x=\frac jN.
\]
Here $\mathbb E$ denotes expectation.

For the concave function $f\left(x\right)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$, the usual
concavity inequality gives
\[
 \mathbb E f\left(U_{\left(j\right)}\right)\le f\left(\mathbb E U_{\left(j\right)}\right)=f\left(j/N\right).
\]
In this case the inequality follows directly from the supporting
tangent at $z=j/N$: for every $u\in\left[0,1\right]$,
\[
 f\left(u\right)\le f\left(z\right)+f'\left(z\right)\left(u-z\right).
\]
Taking expectations cancels the last term because
$\mathbb E U_{\left(j\right)}=z$. Sorting leaves the sum of the values
unchanged for every outcome, so
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{j=1}^{N-1}f\left(j/N\right)
 &\ge\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\mathbb E f\left(U_{\left(j\right)}\right)
   =\mathbb E\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}f\left(U_i\right)\right)\\
 &=\left(N-1\right)\int_0^1f\left(x\right)\,\mathrm d x=\left(N-1\right)I.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Adding $f\left(0\right)=1$ and $f\left(1\right)=0$ gives
$S\left(N\right)-NI\ge1-I$. The case $N=1$ is equality.

For $a\in\left[N,N+1\right]$, with $N\ge1$, the function $S\left(a\right)-Ia$ is
continuous and concave on that closed interval. Indeed, for
$j\ge1$ and $a>j$,
\[
 \frac{\,\mathrm d^2}{\,\mathrm d a^2}\sqrt{1-\frac{j^2}{a^2}}
 =-\frac{j^2\left(3a^2-2j^2\right)}{a^3\left(a^2-j^2\right)^{3/2}}<0,
\]
and the term appearing at the right endpoint has value zero there.
A concave function is no smaller than the minimum of its endpoint
values. The integer estimate therefore proves \eqref{eq:sum}.
If $0<a\le1$, then $S\left(a\right)=1$ and the result is immediate.
Equality at $a=1$ proves optimality of the constant.
head: environment

label: lem:largesum
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:largesum}
For the sum in Lemma~\ref{lem:sum},
\[
 S\left(a\right)\ge\frac\pi4a+\frac{29}{100},\,\,\, a\ge2.
\]
head: environment

label: eq:unittrapezoid
title: Proof
body_md:
For an integer $N\ge2$, put $f_N\left(x\right)=\sqrt{1-\left(x/N\right)^2}$.
The composite trapezoidal rule is the sum of the areas of the
endpoint trapezoids on the $N$ unit intervals:
\[
 T_N:=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\frac{f_N\left(j\right)+f_N\left(j+1\right)}2
     =\frac12f_N\left(0\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}f_N\left(j\right)+\frac12f_N\left(N\right)
     =S\left(N\right)-\frac12.
\]
Here $f_N\left(0\right)=1$ and $f_N\left(N\right)=0$. Since $f_N$ is concave, each
endpoint chord lies below its graph. Therefore
\[
 E_N:=\int_0^N f_N\left(x\right)\,\mathrm d x-T_N\ge0,\qquad
 S\left(N\right)-\frac{\pi N}{4}=\frac12-E_N.
\]
To estimate the error on a unit interval, define
\[
 K_j\left(x\right)=\frac{\left(x-j\right)\left(j+1-x\right)}2
       =\frac18-\frac12\left(x-j-\frac12\right)^2,
       \qquad j\le x\le j+1.
\]
The completed-square expression shows directly that
$0\le K_j\left(x\right)\le1/8$, with its maximum at $x=j+1/2$.
Thus $K_j$ vanishes at the two endpoints,
$K_j'\left(j\right)=1/2$, $K_j'\left(j+1\right)=-1/2$, and $K_j''=-1$.
For a continuously differentiable function $F$ whose derivative
is absolutely continuous on $\left[j,j+1\right]$, two integrations
by parts give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:unittrapezoid}
 \begin{aligned}
 \int_j^{j+1}K_j\left(x\right)F''\left(x\right)\,\mathrm d x
 &=\left[K_jF'\right]_j^{j+1}-\left[K_j'F\right]_j^{j+1}
       +\int_j^{j+1}K_j''\left(x\right)F\left(x\right)\,\mathrm d x\\
 &=\frac{F\left(j\right)+F\left(j+1\right)}2
       -\int_j^{j+1}F\left(x\right)\,\mathrm d x.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For $j=0,\ldots,N-2$, the function $f_N$ is smooth on this interval.
Consequently the concave trapezoidal error on this interval is
\[
 e_j:=\int_j^{j+1}f_N\left(x\right)\,\mathrm d x
           -\frac{f_N\left(j\right)+f_N\left(j+1\right)}2
      =-\int_j^{j+1}K_j\left(x\right)f_N''\left(x\right)\,\mathrm d x.
\]
Since $0\le K_j\le1/8$ and $f_N''\le0$, summing the first
$N-1$ intervals gives
\[
 0\le\sum_{j=0}^{N-2}e_j
 \le-\frac18\int_0^{N-1}f_N''\left(x\right)\,\mathrm d x
 =-\frac{f_N'\left(N-1\right)}8
 =\frac{N-1}{8N\sqrt{2N-1}}.
\]
Indeed $f_N'\left(x\right)=-x/\left(N\sqrt{N^2-x^2}\right)$ and
$f_N''\left(x\right)=-N/\left(N^2-x^2\right)^{3/2}$ for $x<N$.
Since $f_N'\left(x\right)\to-\infty$ as $x\uparrow N$, applying
the derivative-increment bound through the last endpoint would
give no finite estimate. We estimate the last interval directly. With $y=N-x$,
\[
 f_N\left(N-y\right)=\sqrt{\frac{2y}{N}-\frac{y^2}{N^2}}
           \le\sqrt{\frac{2y}{N}},\qquad 0\le y\le1.
\]
As $f_N\left(N-1\right)=\sqrt{2N-1}/N$, this gives
\[
 e_{N-1}
 =\int_0^1f_N\left(N-y\right)\,\mathrm d y-\frac{f_N\left(N-1\right)}2
 \le\frac{2\sqrt2}{3\sqrt N}-\frac{\sqrt{2N-1}}{2N}.
\]
Adding the two bounds proves
\[
 E_N\le\frac{N-1}{8N\sqrt{2N-1}}
          +\frac{2\sqrt2}{3\sqrt N}
          -\frac{\sqrt{2N-1}}{2N}.
\]
For $N\ge2$, use $\left(N-1\right)/N\le1$,
$\sqrt{2N-1}\ge\sqrt N$, and
$\sqrt{2N-1}/N\ge\sqrt{3/2}/\sqrt N$ to obtain
\[
 E_N\le\frac{1/8+2\sqrt2/3-\sqrt{3/2}/2}{\sqrt N}.
\]
The rational comparisons $\sqrt2<99/70$ and
$\sqrt{3/2}>61/50$ bound the numerator by
$641/1400<23/50$. For $N\ge5$, the bound
$\sqrt N\ge\sqrt5>11/5$ therefore gives
\[
 E_N<\frac{23}{110}<\frac{21}{100},\qquad
 S\left(N\right)-\frac{\pi N}{4}>\frac{16}{55}>\frac{29}{100}.
\]

It remains to check $N=2,3,4$. Their sums are
\[
 S\left(2\right)=1+\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\qquad
 S\left(3\right)=1+\frac{2\sqrt2+\sqrt5}{3},\qquad
 S\left(4\right)=1+\frac{\sqrt{15}+2\sqrt3+\sqrt7}{4}.
\]
Using $\pi<22/7$, $\sqrt3>173/100$, $\sqrt2>7/5$,
$\sqrt5>11/5$, $\sqrt{15}>19/5$ and $\sqrt7>13/5$ gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 S\left(2\right)-\frac\pi2
 &>1+\frac{173}{200}-\frac{11}{7}=\frac{411}{1400},\\
 S\left(3\right)-\frac{3\pi}{4}
 &>1+\frac{2\left(7/5\right)+11/5}{3}-\frac{33}{14}=\frac{13}{42},\\
 S\left(4\right)-\pi
 &>1+\frac{19/5+2\left(173/100\right)+13/5}{4}-\frac{22}{7}
   =\frac{451}{1400}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each rational lower bound exceeds $29/100$. Finally, the concavity
of $S\left(a\right)-\pi a/4$ on every $\left[N,N+1\right]$, established in
Lemma~\ref{lem:sum}, extends these integer bounds to every $a\ge2$.

label: prop:mixedlow
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:mixedlow}
Let $0<\delta\le1/4$, $R=1+\delta$, and
\[
 a_\delta=\sqrt{\frac{R^2-1}{2\log R}},\quad
 B_0=2a_\delta-\frac\pi2-\frac\delta\pi,\quad
 B_2=2a_\delta-\frac{71}{50}-\frac\delta\pi.
\]
For $t>\sqrt{3}/2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mixedlow}
 N_A\left(t^2\right)-\frac{R^2-1}{4}t^2
 \ge-\frac{\delta^2}{4}t^2+B_0t-1-\frac{3\delta}{8}.
\end{equation}
If $\delta\sqrt{t^2-3/4}/\pi\ge2$, one may replace $B_0$ by $B_2$.
Moreover
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mixedB}
 B_0>\frac37+\frac35\delta,\,\,\,
 B_2>\frac{29}{50}+\frac{78}{125}\delta.
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
A radially constant trial function in the integer angular order $m$
has Rayleigh quotient
\[
 m^2\frac{\int_1^R s^{-1}\,\mathrm d s}{\int_1^R s\,\mathrm d s}
 =\frac{2m^2\log R}{R^2-1}=\frac{m^2}{a_\delta^2},
\]
so $\lambda_{m,0}\le m^2/a_\delta^2$. The effective radius
$a_\delta$ keeps the exact radial weight in the first row, which
is more accurate than replacing it by the inner radius.
For higher radial rows keep Lemma~\ref{lem:radial}.
Writing $z=\sqrt{t^2-3/4}$ and $A=\delta z/\pi$, the order count
$\#\left\{m\in\mathbb Z:\left|m\right|\le b\right\}\ge2b-1$ gives directly
\[
 N_A\left(t^2\right)\ge2a_\delta t-1+
 \sum_{n=1}^{\left\lfloor A\right\rfloor}
       \left(2z\sqrt{1-\left(n/A\right)^2}-1\right).
\]
The sum over $n\ge1$ counts only higher radial rows; the zeroth
row is supplied by the separate constant trial function. In
particular, negative lower bounds $2b-1$ for individual short
rows are harmless, since their actual counts are nonnegative. Apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:sum} to obtain
\[
 N_A\left(t^2\right)\ge\frac\delta2\left(t^2-3/4\right)+2a_\delta t
                  -\left(\frac\pi2+\frac\delta\pi\right)z-1.
\]
Replacing $z$ by $t$ in the negative term proves
\eqref{eq:mixedlow}. If $A\ge2$, Lemma~\ref{lem:largesum} replaces
$\pi/2$ in that display by $71/50$, proving the stronger assertion.

Writing $L=\log R$, one has
$a_\delta^2=R\sinh\left(L\right)/L\ge R$. On $0\le\delta\le1/4$,
\[
 \sqrt{1+\delta}\ge1+\frac{33}{70}\delta
                         \ge1+\frac7{15}\delta,
\]
as follows by squaring; indeed $33/35+1089/19600<1$.
Together with $3<\pi<22/7$ this proves the first bound in
\eqref{eq:mixedB}. For the second use $\pi>157/50$ and
\[
 \frac{33}{35}-\frac{50}{157}=\frac{3431}{5495}>\frac{78}{125}.
\]

label: lem:actionquadrature
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:actionquadrature}
The action has $f_t'\left(0\right)=0$ and
\[
 2\int_0^{Rt}f_t\left(v\right)\,\mathrm d v=\frac{R^2-1}{4}t^2,
 \,\,\,
 -f_t''\left(v\right)\ge\frac{\delta}{\pi Rt}\quad\left(0\le v<t\right).
\]
For the integer angular multiset $\mathcal V$,
\[
 \left|\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}f_t\left(\left|m\right|\right)
          -\frac{R^2-1}{4}t^2\right|
 \le\tau_\delta:=\frac{\arccos\left(1/R\right)}{2\pi}<\frac14.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Integration by parts gives
\[
 \int_0^1\sqrt{1-x^2}\,\mathrm d x=\frac\pi4,\,\,\,
 \int_0^1x\arccos x\,\mathrm d x=\frac\pi8,
\]
and hence $\int_0^1g\left(x\right)\,\mathrm d x=1/8$. Scaling the two terms in
$\mathcal G_\delta$ now gives the displayed integral identity.
On the core interval,
\[
 -f_t''\left(v\right)=\frac1\pi\left(
 \frac1{\sqrt{t^2-v^2}}-\frac1{\sqrt{R^2t^2-v^2}}\right).
\]
This is increasing in $v$ and takes the value $\delta/\left(\pi Rt\right)$
at zero. The even extension $F_t\left(x\right)=f_t\left(\left|x\right|\right)$, extended by zero
outside $\left[-Rt,Rt\right]$, is $C^1$ and has an integrable second derivative.
The derivative of $f_t$ decreases from zero to
$-\arccos\left(1/R\right)/\pi$ on $\left[0,t\right]$ and increases to zero on $\left[t,Rt\right]$.
Consequently
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_{\mathbb R}\left(F_t'\right)=
 \frac{4\arccos\left(1/R\right)}\pi.
\]
On each unit interval of the integer grid, the trapezoidal
remainder is bounded by one eighth of the integral of $\left|F_t''\right|$.
Summing these bounds gives the stated error, since the full
trapezoidal sum equals $\sum_mF_t\left(m\right)$.
head: environment

label: lem:exactphasecount
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $d_m\left(t\right)=\varphi_m\left(Rt\right)-\varphi_m\left(t\right)$ and consider
\[
 u_t\left(s\right)=Y_m'\left(t\right)J_m\left(ts\right)-J_m'\left(t\right)Y_m\left(ts\right).
\]
The Bessel Wronskian identity
$J_m\left(x\right)Y_m'\left(x\right)-J_m'\left(x\right)Y_m\left(x\right)=2/\left(\pi x\right)$
\cite[(10.5.2)]{NIST} gives $u_t\left(1\right)=2/\left(\pi t\right)>0$ and
$\partial_su_t\left(1\right)=0$, while
\[
 \partial_su_t\left(R\right)=-t\mathcal M_m\left(t\right)\mathcal M_m\left(Rt\right)\sin d_m\left(t\right).
\]
The right Neumann condition is therefore equivalent to
$\sin d_m\left(t\right)=0$, or $d_m\left(t\right)=j\pi$ for an integer $j$.
Geometrically, the derivative vectors at $t$ and $Rt$ are then
parallel or antiparallel. Their angle must be followed on the
continuous branch in Figure~\ref{fig:derivativephase}; retaining
the number of turns is what turns this boundary condition into
a spectral count. Thus positive radial eigenvalues occur exactly
at the integer levels of $d_m/\pi$. The single minimum property of $\varphi_m$ implies
$d_m\left(t\right)>-\pi/2$. For $m>0$, $d_m\left(t\right)<0$ at small positive $t$;
for $m=0$, $d_0\left(t\right)>0$ and tends to zero as $t\downarrow0$.

To turn this zero condition into an exact count, it remains to
check the direction of each crossing. Every crossing of an
integer level is positive. To see this,
suppose $d_m\left(t\right)=j\pi$. The Wronskian identity gives
\[
 u_t\left(R\right)=\left(-1\right)^j\frac{\mathcal M_m\left(t\right)}{\mathcal M_m\left(Rt\right)}
                       \frac2{\pi Rt}.
\]
Normalize $u_t\left(1\right)=1$ by a positive scalar and write
$z=\partial_\lambda u_t$, where $\lambda=t^2$. The radial
equation is $-\left(su_t'\right)'+m^2s^{-1}u_t=\lambda su_t$.
Multiply its differentiated equation by $u_t$, subtract the
original equation multiplied by $z$, and integrate. Because
$z\left(1\right)=z'\left(1\right)=u_t'\left(R\right)=0$ at an eigenvalue, the boundary terms give
\[
 -Ru_t\left(R\right)\,\partial_\lambda\partial_su_t\left(R\right)
       =\int_1^R s\,u_t\left(s\right)^2\,\mathrm d s>0.
\]
At the root the derivatives of the prefactor multiplying
$\sin d_m$ vanish from the expression, because $\sin d_m=0$.
Since $\partial_\lambda d_m=d_m'\left(t\right)/\left(2t\right)$, differentiating the
right derivative gives a positive prefactor times
$-\left(-1\right)^j d_m'\left(t\right)$. The value $u_t\left(R\right)$ has sign $\left(-1\right)^j$,
so the positive left-hand side of the preceding identity has
the sign of $d_m'\left(t\right)$. Therefore $d_m'\left(t\right)>0$.
Positive radial eigenvalues are simple for this regular
one-dimensional boundary problem \cite{Davies}.
Starting with $-1/2<d_m\left(t\right)/\pi<0$ for $m>0$, or with
$0<d_0\left(t\right)/\pi\ll1$ for $m=0$, each encountered integer level
therefore adds exactly one eigenvalue. Continuity proves
\eqref{eq:exactphasecount}, including equality
at an eigenvalue. The extra initial count for $m=0$ is precisely its
zero eigenvalue. No global monotonicity of $d_m$ is needed.
head: environment

label: lem:globalphaseerror
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:globalphaseerror}
For integers $m\ge1$ and $t\ge m$, and also for $m=0$
and $t\ge2$,
\[
 0\le e_m\left(t\right):=\varphi_m\left(t\right)-A_m\left(t\right)-\pi/4<\sqrt{3/2}<3/2<\pi/2.
\]
At $t=m$ the expression is understood by continuity.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[Lemma~1.8]{Phase}, the minimum of the raw upper
envelope decreases with the order. Therefore
\[
 z_m^*\le z_0^*=\frac\pi4+\sqrt{\frac32}.
\]
For $m<x<x_m^*$, the constant part of the enclosure in
\cite[Theorem~1.10]{Phase} and $A_m\left(x\right)\ge0$ give
\[
 e_m\left(x\right)
 <z_m^*-A_m\left(x\right)-\frac\pi4
 \le\sqrt{\frac32}.
\]
For $x\ge x_m^*$, use the raw upper bound and the monotonicity
\[
 E_m'\left(x\right)=
 -\frac{x\left(3x^2+4m^2\right)}
 {8\left(x^2-m^2\right)^{5/2}}<0
\]
to obtain
\[
 e_m\left(x\right)<E_m\left(x\right)
 \le E_m\left(x_m^*\right)
 =z_m^*-A_m\left(x_m^*\right)-\frac\pi4
 \le\sqrt{\frac32}.
\]
For $m\ge1$, strict increase of the actual phase on
$\left(m,x_m^*\right)$ gives
$\varphi_m\left(m\right)<\varphi_m\left(x_m^*\right)<z_m^*$,
so the same strict upper bound holds at $x=m$.
The nonnegative lower bound follows from the lower phase
enclosure and continuity. Thus
$0\le e_m\left(x\right)<\sqrt{3/2}<3/2<\pi/2$
on the stated range, since $\pi>3$.
head: environment

label: lem:bvsample
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:bvsample}
Let $f\in C^1\left(\left[0,T\right]\right)$ have absolutely continuous derivative, with
$f'\left(0\right)=0$ and $f''\le-\kappa<0$ almost everywhere. For every
$b\in\mathbb R$,
\[
 \left|\int_0^T\psi\left(f\left(x\right)+b\right)\,\mathrm d x\right|
 \le\frac1{2\sqrt\kappa}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The continuous periodic function
\[
 \mathcal P\left(y\right)=\frac12\left(\left\{y\right\}-1/2\right)^2-\frac1{16},
 \,\,\, \left|\mathcal P\left(y\right)\right|\le\frac1{16},
\]
is a primitive of $\psi$ almost everywhere. For $0<s<T$, integrate
by parts with $\mathcal P\left(f+b\right)/f'$. Since $f'<0$ and $1/f'$ is
increasing, its endpoint and variation contributions give
\[
 \left|\int_s^T\psi\left(f\left(x\right)+b\right)\,\mathrm d x\right|
 \le\frac1{8\left|f'\left(s\right)\right|}\le\frac1{8\kappa s}.
\]
Indeed, writing $H=1/f'$, the bound is
$\left(\left|H\left(s\right)\right|+\left|H\left(T\right)\right|+\operatorname{Var}_{\left[s,T\right]}H\right)/16
=\left|H\left(s\right)\right|/8$, because $H<0$ is increasing. The initial integral
has absolute value at most $s/2$, because $\left|\psi\right|\le1/2$.
Thus, whenever $0<s<T$,
\[
 \left|\int_0^T\psi\left(f\left(x\right)+b\right)\,\mathrm d x\right|
 \le\frac{s}{2}+\frac{1}{8\kappa s}.
\]
The right-hand side is minimized at $s=1/\left(2\sqrt\kappa\right)$,
where its two terms are both $1/\left(4\sqrt\kappa\right)$. Their sum
is $1/\left(2\sqrt\kappa\right)$. If this choice is at least $T$, the
direct bound $T/2\le1/\left(4\sqrt\kappa\right)$ suffices instead. An integrable
singularity of $f''$ at $T$ is handled by taking a limit from below.
head: environment

label: lem:combinedgrid
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:combinedgrid}
Let $v$ be a left-continuous function of bounded variation on $\left[0,T\right]$,
with its actual value at zero retained. For the multiset
$\mathcal V=\left\{\left|m\right|:m\in\mathbb Z\right\}$,
\[
 \left|\sum_{x\in\mathcal V\cap\left[0,T\right]}v\left(x\right)
                 -2\int_0^T v\left(x\right)\,\mathrm d x\right|
 \le\operatorname{Var}_{\left[0,T\right]}v+\left|v\left(T\right)\right|.
\]
Consequently, if $q$ satisfies the regularity and curvature
assumptions of Lemma~\ref{lem:bvsample} with curvature $\kappa$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:combinedsaw}
 \left|\sum_{x\in\mathcal V\cap\left[0,T\right]}\psi\left(q\left(x\right)\right)\right|
 \le\kappa^{-1/2}+2\left(q\left(0\right)-q\left(T\right)\right)+\frac32.
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The integer-grid discrepancy
\[
 \mathcal D\left(x\right)=\#\left\{m\in\mathbb Z:\left|m\right|\le x\right\}-2x
              =2\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor+1-2x,\qquad x\ge0.
\]
There are $\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor$ positive orders, the same number of
negative orders, and one zero order. Hence
$\mathcal D\left(x\right)=1-2\left\{x\right\}$, which lies in $\left(-1,1\right]$ and has
absolute value at most one. Let $\sigma$ be the signed
Lebesgue--Stieltjes measure encoding the increments of the
left-continuous $v$: $\sigma\left(\left[x,y\right)\right)=v\left(y\right)-v\left(x\right)$ for $0\le x<y\le T$.
This includes a possible right jump at zero. Indeed
$v\left(x\right)=v\left(T\right)-\sigma\left(\left[x,T\right)\right)$. Integrate this identity against the
signed measure consisting of the angular point masses minus
$2\,\mathrm d x$, and exchange the finite measure integrals. The inner
measure of $\left[0,y\right]$ is exactly $\mathcal D\left(y\right)$, giving the exact error
\[
 v\left(T\right)\mathcal D\left(T\right)-\int_{\left[0,T\right)}\mathcal D\left(x\right)\,\mathrm d\sigma\left(x\right).
\]
This proves the first assertion with the stated endpoint convention.
We justify the variation identity with the endpoint convention
used in the preceding Stieltjes calculation. For $T=0$ the
identity is immediate, so suppose $T>0$. The assumptions on $q$
imply $q'\left(x\right)\le-\kappa x<0$ for $x>0$, hence $q$ is strictly
decreasing. It is also continuously differentiable and therefore
absolutely continuous on $\left[0,T\right]$. Put $\Delta=q\left(0\right)-q\left(T\right)$ and
define the finite crossing set
\[
 \mathcal C=\left\{x\in\left[0,T\right):q\left(x\right)\in\mathbb Z\right\}.
\]
Each integer in $\left(q\left(T\right),q\left(0\right)\right]$ has exactly one preimage in
$\mathcal C$, by continuity and strict decrease. Thus
\[
 J=\#\mathcal C
  =\left\lfloor q\left(0\right)\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor q\left(T\right)\right\rfloor.
\]
With $h\left(x\right)=\psi\left(q\left(x\right)\right)=q\left(x\right)-\left\lfloor q\left(x\right)\right\rfloor-1/2$, an
integer crossing has value $h\left(x\right)=-1/2$ and right limit
$h\left(x+\right)=1/2$. Its left limit agrees with its value. Between
crossings, $h'=q'$. More explicitly, for $0\le x<y\le T$,
\[
 h\left(y\right)-h\left(x\right)
  =\int_x^y q'\left(s\right)\,\,\mathrm d s
      +\#\left(\mathcal C\cap\left[x,y\right)\right).
\]
An integer at the initial endpoint is included in this formula,
whereas an integer at $y$ has not yet produced its right jump.
The signed Stieltjes measure associated with these increments
is consequently
\[
 \,\mathrm d\sigma_h=q'\left(x\right)\,\,\mathrm d x+\sum_{c\in\mathcal C}\delta_c
 \quad\hbox{on }\left[0,T\right),
\]
where $\delta_c$ denotes the unit point mass at $c$. Its absolutely
continuous part is nonpositive and its atomic part is positive;
the two parts are mutually singular. Its total variation is
therefore the sum of their masses:
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_{\left[0,T\right]}h
 =-\int_0^T q'\left(x\right)\,\,\mathrm d x+J
 =q\left(0\right)-q\left(T\right)+J=\Delta+J.
\]
A crossing at zero contributes one right jump; a crossing at $T$
produces no jump outside the interval. Finally,
\[
 J=\Delta+\left\{q\left(T\right)\right\}-\left\{q\left(0\right)\right\}<\Delta+1,
 \qquad \left|h\left(T\right)\right|\le\frac12,
\]
so the non-strict estimate $\operatorname{Var}_{\left[0,T\right]}h\le2\Delta+1$
used in the lemma is valid.

The first assertion of the lemma and the continuous integral
estimate now give the complete chain
\[
 \left|\sum_{x\in\mathcal V\cap\left[0,T\right]}h\left(x\right)\right|
 \le2\left|\int_0^T h\left(x\right)\,\mathrm d x\right|
       +\operatorname{Var}_{\left[0,T\right]}h+\left|h\left(T\right)\right|
 \le\kappa^{-1/2}+2\Delta+\frac32.
\]
This is \eqref{eq:combinedsaw}. The density two accounts for the
factor before the integral. The zero order is counted once and
each positive integer order twice, as encoded in $\mathcal D$.
head: environment

label: prop:explicitcount
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:explicitcount}
Let $0<\delta\le1/4$, $R=1+\delta$ and $t\ge2$. Put
\[
 d_\delta=\delta-\sqrt{R^2-1}+\arccos\left(1/R\right),\quad
 L_\delta=1-\frac\delta2-\frac{2d_\delta}{\pi},\quad
 \tau_\delta=\frac{\arccos\left(1/R\right)}{2\pi},
\]
and, with $T=t-1$,
\[
 \eta_t\left(x\right)=\frac{9t^2-2x^2}{24\pi\left(t^2-x^2\right)^{3/2}},\,\,\,
 I_t=\int_0^T\eta_t\left(x\right)\,\mathrm d x
 =\frac{7T/\sqrt{t^2-T^2}+2\arcsin\left(T/t\right)}{24\pi}.
\]
Then, for the ordinary Neumann count,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:explicitcount}
 N_A\left(t^2\right)-\frac{R^2-1}{4}t^2
 \ge L_\delta t-\sqrt{\frac{\pi Rt}{\delta}}
          -2I_t-4\eta_t\left(T\right)-\frac{9}{2}-\tau_\delta.
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The action $f_t$ has $f_t'\left(0\right)=0$, $-f_t''\ge\kappa=\delta/\left(\pi Rt\right)$
on $\left[0,t\right)$, and the exact variation
\[
 f_t\left(0\right)-f_t\left(t\right)=\frac{d_\delta}{\pi}t.
\]
On $\left[0,T\right]$ put $q=f_t-\eta_t$. The function $\eta_t$ is increasing
and convex, with derivative zero at zero: after setting $s=x/t$,
its numerator can be written as
$7\left(1-s^2\right)^{-3/2}+2\left(1-s^2\right)^{-1/2}$, divided by $24\pi t$.
Hence $q'\left(0\right)=0$ and $q''\le-\kappa$.
The exact phase identity and \eqref{eq:phaseinput} give
\[
 n_v\left(t^2\right)\ge\left\lfloor f_t\left(v\right)-\eta_t\left(v\right)\right\rfloor+1
 \quad\left(0\le v\le T\right).
\]
For the remaining core orders $T<v\le t$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:globalphaseerror} gives $e_v\left(t\right)/\pi<1/2$,
and hence $n_v\left(t^2\right)\ge f_t\left(v\right)-1/2$.
For $t<v\le Rt$, the one-sided outer comparison gives
$n_v\left(t^2\right)\ge f_t\left(v\right)-1/4$.

Let $N_c,N_o,N_b$ count angular orders, with multiplicity, in
$\left[0,t\right]$, $\left(t,Rt\right]$, and $\left(T,t\right]$, respectively. If
$C\left(b\right)=\#\left\{m\in\mathbb Z:\left|m\right|\le b\right\}$, then $\left|C\left(b\right)-2b\right|\le1$.
Consequently
$N_c/2-N_o/4=3C\left(t\right)/4-C\left(Rt\right)/4
\ge\left(1-\delta/2\right)t-1$. The half-open interval
$\left(t-1,t\right]$ contains exactly the positive integer $\left\lfloor t\right\rfloor$;
its angular multiplicity is two. Hence
\[
 \frac12N_c-\frac14N_o\ge\left(1-\delta/2\right)t-1,
 \,\,\, N_b=2.
\]
The total action sum differs from its integral $\left(R^2-1\right)t^2/4$
by at most $\tau_\delta$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:actionquadrature}.
To apply Lemma~\ref{lem:combinedgrid}, keep the full angular
multiset: the sum below means
$\psi\left(q\left(0\right)\right)+2\sum_{j=1}^{\left\lfloor T\right\rfloor}\psi\left(q\left(j\right)\right)$.
The action decreases and $T<t$, while
$\eta_t\left(0\right)=3/\left(8\pi t\right)>0$. Thus
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Delta=q\left(0\right)-q\left(T\right)
 &=f_t\left(0\right)-f_t\left(T\right)+\eta_t\left(T\right)-\eta_t\left(0\right)\\
 &\le f_t\left(0\right)-f_t\left(t\right)+\eta_t\left(T\right)-\eta_t\left(0\right)\\
 &\le\frac{d_\delta}{\pi}t+\eta_t\left(T\right).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Substituting this bound and $\kappa=\delta/\left(\pi Rt\right)$ into
\eqref{eq:combinedsaw} gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \left|\sum_{v\le T}\psi\left(q\left(v\right)\right)\right|
 &\le\kappa^{-1/2}+2\Delta+\frac32\\
 &\le\sqrt{\frac{\pi Rt}{\delta}}
       +\frac{2d_\delta}{\pi}t+2\eta_t\left(T\right)+\frac32.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The constant $3/2$ is the sum of the jump-count allowance $1$
and the endpoint allowance $1/2$; it is not a lost angular mode.
The same discrepancy formula applied to the smooth increasing
$\eta_t$ gives
\[
 \sum_{v\le T}\eta_t\left(v\right)\le2I_t+2\eta_t\left(T\right).
\]
In the far core use
$\left\lfloor q\right\rfloor+1=f_t-\eta_t+1/2-\psi\left(q\right)$.
In the band the preceding lower bound loses at most one relative
to the nonoscillatory contribution $f_t+1/2$. Combining these
estimates, with $1+2+3/2=9/2$, proves \eqref{eq:explicitcount}.
All sums retain the angular multiplicities.
head: environment

label: prop:explicitjoin
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:explicitjoin}
For every $0<\delta\le1/4$,
\[
 N_A\left(\Lambda\right)>\frac{\delta\left(2+\delta\right)}4\Lambda
 \,\,\,\left(\Lambda\ge0\right).
\]
The comparison estimates meet at
\[
 t_0=\frac{2+\left(10/3\right)\delta}{\delta^2}\ge\frac{136}{3}.
\]
For $t\ge t_0$, their high-frequency excess is greater than $49t/1000$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First consider high frequencies. The function $d_\delta$ increases,
since $d_\delta'=1-\sqrt{R^2-1}/R>0$; thus $L_\delta$ decreases.
At $\delta=1/4$, set $\theta=\arccos\left(4/5\right)$. The identity
$\theta=\pi/4-\arctan\left(1/7\right)$ and the alternating arctangent bound give
\[
 \theta<\frac{11}{14}-\left(\frac17-\frac1{1029}\right)
 =\frac{1325}{2058}<\frac{161}{250}.
\]
Consequently, using $\pi>157/50$,
\[
 L_\delta\ge\frac78-\frac{2\theta-1}{\pi}
 >\frac{4919}{6280}>\frac{783}{1000}.
\]
The function $\delta\left(1+\delta\right)/\left(2+\left(10/3\right)\delta\right)$ increases.
For $t\ge t_0$ we therefore have
\[
 \sqrt{\frac{\pi R}{\delta t}}
 \le\sqrt{\frac{15\pi}{136}}<\frac{589}{1000};
\]
the last comparison follows from
$15\pi/136<165/476<\left(589/1000\right)^2$.
Since $t\ge136/3$ and $\sqrt{269/3}>47/5$, the exact formula for
$I_t$ gives
\[
 \frac{2I_t}{t}\le\frac7{12\pi\sqrt{2t-1}}+\frac1{12t}
 <\frac{20}{1000}+\frac2{1000}.
\]
Also $\left(7t+4\right)/\left(2t-1\right)^{3/2}$ decreases, so
\[
 \frac{4\eta_t\left(t-1\right)}{t}
 \le\frac{7t+4}{6\pi\left(2t-1\right)^{3/2}}
 <\frac{120500}{5954853}<\frac{21}{1000}.
\]
Finally $\tau_\delta<161/1570$, and
\[
 \frac{9/2+\tau_\delta}{t}
 <\frac{10839}{106760}<\frac{102}{1000}.
\]
The total normalized loss in \eqref{eq:explicitcount} is less than
$\left(589+20+2+21+102\right)/1000=734/1000$. The normalized excess is
therefore greater than $49/1000$.

For low frequencies put $t_1=7/\delta<t_0$. The number seven
is chosen so that the higher-row parameter exceeds two throughout
$\left[t_1,+\infty\right)$: it is a simple rational number larger than
$2\pi$ with room for the correction $3\delta^2/4$.
On $\left[3,t_1\right]$, the first bound in \eqref{eq:mixedB} makes the
right-hand side of \eqref{eq:mixedlow} a concave quadratic.
Its value at $3$ is bounded below by
\[
 \frac27+\frac{57}{40}\delta-\frac94\delta^2>\frac27,
\]
and at $t_1$ it is at least
\[
 \frac3\delta-\frac{181}{20}-\frac{3\delta}{8}
 \ge\frac{457}{160}>0.
\]
For $t\ge t_1$, the hypothesis for the stronger row bound holds:
$\delta\sqrt{t^2-3/4}\ge\sqrt{49-3\delta^2/4}>2\pi$.
Writing $c=2+\left(10/3\right)\delta$, the second bound in
\eqref{eq:mixedB} gives
\[
 B_2-\frac c4>\frac2{25}-\frac{157}{750}\delta
 \ge\frac{83}{3000}.
\]
At $t_0=c/\delta^2$ the stronger quadratic excess is consequently
at least
\[
 \frac{83}{3000}\frac{136}{3}-\frac{35}{32}
 =\frac{5777}{36000}>0.
\]
The stronger quadratic is larger than the weaker one because
$B_2>B_0$, as $\pi/2>71/50$. It is therefore positive at $t_1$
as well. A concave function on an interval is bounded below by
the smaller of its endpoint values, which covers $\left[t_1,t_0\right]$.

For $t\le1$, the area term is at most $9/64<1$, and the zero mode supplies a
count for every $t\ge0$. For $1\le t\le3$ the
zeroth radial row gives $N_A\left(t^2\right)\ge2a_\delta t-1\ge t$,
whereas $\left(R^2-1\right)t^2/4\le27t/64<t$. This covers the remaining
energies and completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Proposition~\ref{prop:explicitjoin} gives the strict counting estimate
when the inner radius is one. Scaling lengths by $r$ replaces
$\Lambda$ by $r^2\Lambda$ and $R$ by $R/r$, giving
\[
 N_A\left(\Lambda\right)>\frac{R^2-r^2}{4}\Lambda.
\]
At $\Lambda=4k/\left(R^2-r^2\right)$ the right-hand side is the integer $k$,
so at least $k+1$ eigenvalues, including the zero mode, lie at or below
this energy. This is the asserted bound on $\nu_k$.
head: environment

label: lem:outerfloors
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:outerfloors}
Use the disk action $G_U$ defined in \eqref{eq:diskaction}. Suppose $U\ge2$, $0\le t<U$, and a unit
grid has first point $a>t$ and $n$ points in $\left[a,U\right]$. Then
\[
 \sum_{\substack{j\ge0\\a+j\le U}}
       \left\lfloor G_U\left(a+j\right)+3/4\right\rfloor
 \ge\sum_{\substack{j\ge0\\a+j\le U}}G_U\left(a+j\right)
       +\frac n4-\frac12G_U\left(t\right)-\frac38U^{1/3}-\frac5{16}.
\]
The assertion also holds for an empty grid.
head: environment

label: fig:trapezoid
title: Proof
body_md:
The quarter-height inverse is taken on $\left[0,U\right]$, where $G_U$ is
continuous and strictly decreasing. It exists because
$G_U\left(0\right)=U/\pi>1/4$ for $U\ge2$, whereas $G_U\left(U\right)=0$. Write
$x_*=G_U^{-1}\left(1/4\right)$ and $w_0=U-x_*$. The level $1/4$ is
dictated by the shift $3/4$: a height $z\ge0$ contributes
zero to $\left\lfloor z+3/4\right\rfloor$ precisely when $z<1/4$.
It is unrelated to the relative-width restriction in the thin
annulus theorem. The lower tail estimate
$w_0>1$ is the established bound of
\cite[Lemma~4.8]{FLPSballs}; we spell out its calculation to verify
the hypothesis needed for the floor-sum theorem.
Set
\[
 \theta_U=\arccos\left(1-\frac1U\right),\qquad
 H\left(U\right)=G_U\left(U-1\right)
     =\frac{\sqrt{2U-1}-\left(U-1\right)\theta_U}{\pi}.
\]
Differentiation gives
\[
 H'\left(U\right)=\frac{\sin\theta_U-\theta_U}{\pi}<0,
 \qquad \sin\theta_U=\frac{\sqrt{2U-1}}U.
\]
The last inequality follows from $\sin\theta<\theta$ for
$\theta>0$. Furthermore,
\[
 H\left(2\right)=\frac{\sqrt3}{\pi}-\frac13<\frac14;
\]
for example, $\pi>3$ and $\sqrt3<7/4$ suffice for this comparison.
Thus $G_U\left(U-1\right)<1/4=G_U\left(x_*\right)$. Strict decrease gives
$x_*<U-1$, or $w_0>1$.

The upper tail bound follows independently from the action
integral and $\arccos\left(1-z\right)\ge\sqrt{2z}$ for $0\le z\le1$:
\[
 \frac14=G_U\left(U-w_0\right)
 \ge\frac1\pi\int_{U-w_0}^{U}
       \sqrt{\frac{2\left(U-s\right)}U}\,\,\mathrm d s
 =\frac{2\sqrt2}{3\pi\sqrt U}w_0^{3/2}.
\]
Solving for $w_0$ gives
\[
 1<w_0\le\left(\frac{9\pi^2}{128}\right)^{1/3}U^{1/3}
       <U^{1/3}.
\]
The last coefficient is less than one, since
$\pi<22/7$ implies $9\pi^2<128$. The threshold $U\ge2$
is sufficient for these estimates; no optimal threshold is claimed.

If the grid is empty, then $n=0$ and both sums vanish. The
remaining terms on the right-hand side of the lemma are
nonpositive, so the assertion holds. If the grid is nonempty
but $a=U$, then $b=U-a=0$, $n=1$, and the only summand in each
sum is zero. The right-hand side is
\[
 -\frac12G_U\left(t\right)-\frac38U^{1/3}-\frac1{16}<0,
\]
which settles this degenerate interval without using a theorem
whose hypothesis requires $b>0$.

We may therefore suppose $a<U$, so that $b=U-a>0$. The profile
$g\left(y\right)=G_U\left(a+y\right)$ on $\left[0,b\right]$ satisfies
\[
 g'\left(y\right)=-\frac1\pi\arccos\left(\frac{a+y}{U}\right),\qquad
 g''\left(y\right)=\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{U^2-\left(a+y\right)^2}}>0
 \quad\left(0\le y<b\right).
\]
It is nonnegative, strictly decreasing, convex, vanishes at $b$,
and has Lipschitz constant at most $1/2$, since $a>t\ge0$.
If $g\left(0\right)\ge1/4$, its quarter-height abscissa is
\[
 g^{-1}\left(1/4\right)=x_*-a=b-w_0\ge0.
\]
The integer index in \cite[Theorem~6.1]{FLPSballs} is therefore
\[
 M_0=1+\left\lfloor b-w_0\right\rfloor.
\]
Indeed $g\left(j\right)\ge1/4$ is equivalent to $j\le b-w_0$, including
equality at the quarter height. The bounds for the floor function
and $w_0>1$ give
\[
 b-w_0<M_0\le b-w_0+1<b.
\]
Thus $M_0\le b$, as required by the cited theorem, including the
case $g\left(0\right)=1/4$, where $b=w_0>1$ and $M_0=1$. That theorem gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{j=0}^{\left\lfloor b\right\rfloor}\left\lfloor g\left(j\right)+\frac34\right\rfloor
 &\ge\int_0^b g\left(y\right)\,\,\mathrm d y-\frac{b-3M_0}{8}\\
 &=\int_0^b g\left(y\right)\,\,\mathrm d y+\frac b4-\frac38\left(b-M_0\right)\\
 &\ge\int_0^b g\left(y\right)\,\,\mathrm d y+\frac b4-\frac{3w_0}{8}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
If instead $g\left(0\right)<1/4$, then $b<w_0$. Convexity puts the graph
below the chord from $\left(0,g\left(0\right)\right)$ to $\left(b,0\right)$, and hence
\[
 \int_0^b g\left(y\right)\,\,\mathrm d y\le\frac{b\,g\left(0\right)}2<\frac b8.
\]
The proposed lower bound is consequently less than
$3\left(b-w_0\right)/8<0$, while every floor summand is nonnegative.
It therefore holds in this case as well.

We next compare the integral with the action sum. The derivative
formulas above give $g\left(b\right)=g'\left(b\right)=0$ and $-g'\left(0\right)\le1/2$.
Put $M=\left\lceil b\right\rceil$ and extend $g$ by zero from $b$ to $M$.
Its derivative remains continuous at $b$; the displayed square-root
singularity of $g''$ is integrable, so $g'$ remains absolutely
continuous and there is no additional jump term at $b$.

We use the unit-interval error identity derived in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:largesum}, now with a convex profile. The
trapezoidal error has the opposite sign: on $\left[j,j+1\right]$,
\[
 E_j:=\frac{g\left(j\right)+g\left(j+1\right)}2-\int_j^{j+1}g\left(y\right)\,\mathrm d y
 =\frac12\int_j^{j+1}\left(y-j\right)\left(j+1-y\right)g''\left(y\right)\,\mathrm d y.
\]
The endpoint chord lies above the convex profile. By
\eqref{eq:unittrapezoid}, its kernel is the same $K_j$, bounded by
$1/8$. Figure~\ref{fig:trapezoid}
shows the chord error and this kernel. Summing the interval errors gives
\[
 0\le\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}E_j
 \le\frac18\int_0^M g''\left(y\right)\,\mathrm d y
 =\frac{g'\left(M\right)-g'\left(0\right)}8=-\frac{g'\left(0\right)}8\le\frac1{16}.
\]
The trapezoidal sum weights the first endpoint by one half,
and every endpoint at or beyond $b$ has value zero. Hence, whether
$b$ is an integer or not,
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{M-1}\frac{g\left(j\right)+g\left(j+1\right)}2
 =\sum_{j=0}^{\left\lfloor b\right\rfloor}g\left(j\right)-\frac12g\left(0\right),
 \qquad \int_0^M g\left(y\right)\,\mathrm d y=\int_0^b g\left(y\right)\,\mathrm d y.
\]
Combining the last two displays yields
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{\left\lfloor b\right\rfloor}g\left(j\right)

Write $S=\sum_{j=0}^{\left\lfloor b\right\rfloor}g\left(j\right)$. The trapezoidal
estimate just proved yields
\[
 \int_0^b g\left(y\right)\,\,\mathrm d y\ge S-\frac12g\left(0\right)-\frac1{16}.
\]
Since $n=\left\lfloor b\right\rfloor+1$, we have $b\ge n-1$; also
$g\left(0\right)=G_U\left(a\right)\le G_U\left(t\right)$. Combining the estimates gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{j=0}^{\left\lfloor b\right\rfloor}\left\lfloor g\left(j\right)+\frac34\right\rfloor
 &\ge S+\frac b4-\frac12g\left(0\right)-\frac38w_0-\frac1{16}\\
 &\ge S+\frac n4-\frac12G_U\left(t\right)-\frac38U^{1/3}-\frac5{16}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here $5/16=1/4+1/16$: the first term accounts for converting
the interval length to the number of grid points, and the second
is the trapezoidal error. Besides the stated unit-grid assumptions,
only $U\ge2$ and $0\le t<U$ were used.
In particular, this lemma imposes no upper bound on the relative
width of an annulus.

label: prop:allratioestimate
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:allratioestimate}
Normalize the inner radius to one, set $R=1+\delta>1$, and let
$U=Rt$. For $t\ge2$, for the ordinary Neumann counting function,
\begin{align}
 N_A\left(t^2\right)-\frac{R^2-1}{4}t^2
 \ge{}&\mathcal L_\delta t-\sqrt{\frac{\pi Rt}{\delta}}
       -2I_t-4\eta_t\left(t-1\right)-\frac34U^{1/3}-\frac{39}{8},\label{eq:allratioestimate}
\end{align}
where
\[
 \mathcal L_\delta=1+\frac\delta2-\frac{2\delta}\pi
 +\frac{\sqrt{R^2-1}-\arccos\left(1/R\right)}\pi.
\]
Moreover, with $a_*=1/2-1/\pi$ and $b_*=2/\pi$,
\[
 \mathcal L_\delta>a_*R+b_*,\,\,\,
 a_*>9/50,\quad b_*>7/11.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Keep the variable-phase comparison on $0\le v\le t-1$ from
Proposition~\ref{prop:explicitcount}. The core argument uses only
the phase bounds and Lemma~\ref{lem:actionquadrature}, which hold
for every $R>1$; its validity does not require $\delta\le1/4$. Apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:outerfloors} to each angular grid in $\left(t,Rt\right]$.
Here $N_c$ and $N_o$ are the numbers of angular orders, with
multiplicities, in $\left[0,t\right]$ and $\left(t,U\right]$. The two outer contributions
are at least their action sum plus
$N_o/4-f_t\left(t\right)-\left(3/4\right)U^{1/3}-5/8$.
Indeed, apply the preceding lemma to the two identical positive-order
grids; $G_U\left(t\right)=f_t\left(t\right)$ and each grid contributes the term
$-G_U\left(t\right)/2$. Direct integer counting gives
\[
 \frac{N_c}{2}+\frac{N_o}{4}
 =\frac{\left\lfloor t\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor U\right\rfloor+1}{2}
 \ge\frac{t+U-1}{2}.
\]
With $T=t-1$, the estimates used in
Proposition~\ref{prop:explicitcount} give, in the core,
\[
 \sum_{v\le T}\eta_t\left(v\right)\le2I_t+2\eta_t\left(T\right),\,\,\,
 \left|\sum_{v\le T}\psi\left(f_t\left(v\right)-\eta_t\left(v\right)\right)\right|
 \le\sqrt{\frac{\pi Rt}{\delta}}
       +2\left(f_t\left(0\right)-f_t\left(t\right)\right)+2\eta_t\left(T\right)+\frac32.
\]
The sums are over the angular multiset $\mathcal V$. The strip
$\left(T,t\right]$ contains two angular modes and costs at most two relative to the core contribution
$f_t+1/2$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:actionquadrature}, replacing the full
action sum by its integral costs less than $1/4$. Consequently
the constant loss is bounded by
$1/2+5/8+3/2+2+1/4=39/8$.
The linear term is
\[
 \frac{R+1}{2}t-2\left(f_t\left(0\right)-f_t\left(t\right)\right)-f_t\left(t\right)
 =\mathcal L_\delta t,
\]
since $f_t\left(0\right)=\delta t/\pi$ and
$f_t\left(t\right)=t\left(\sqrt{R^2-1}-\arccos\left(1/R\right)\right)/\pi$.
This proves
\eqref{eq:allratioestimate} without a restriction on $\delta$.

For the affine lower bound observe that
\[
 \mathcal L_\delta-a_*R-b_*
 =\frac12-\frac{R-\sqrt{R^2-1}+\arccos\left(1/R\right)}\pi>0.
\]
The expression $R-\sqrt{R^2-1}+\arccos\left(1/R\right)$ has derivative
$1-\sqrt{R^2-1}/R>0$ and tends to $\pi/2$ as
$R\to+\infty$. The rational bounds follow from
$157/50<\pi<22/7$.

label: eq:diskbracketinginner
title: Proof
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{thm:thinall} already covers $\delta\le1/4$.
For the other annuli normalize $r=1$, write $U=Rt\ge80$, and
put $\rho=1/R\le4/5$. First suppose $t\ge2$.
For all such $t$, the exact correction formulas in
Proposition~\ref{prop:allratioestimate} give
\[
 2I_t<\frac16\sqrt t+\frac1{12},\,\,\,
 4\eta_t\left(t-1\right)<\frac13\sqrt t.
\]
For the first inequality use
$\left(t-1\right)/\sqrt{2t-1}\le\sqrt{t/2}$ and
$\arcsin\left(1-1/t\right)\le\pi/2$ in the expression for $I_t$.
Then $7/\left(12\pi\sqrt2\right)<1/6$. For the second bound use
\[
 4\eta_t\left(t-1\right)=
 \frac{7+4/t-2/t^2}{6\pi\left(2-1/t\right)^{3/2}}\sqrt t,
\]
whose numerator is at most nine and denominator greater than 27.

If $\rho\le1/2$, then the curvature term is less than
$\left(251/100\right)\sqrt t$, since
$\pi/\left(1-\rho\right)\le2\pi<\left(251/100\right)^2$.
The total square-root loss is therefore less than
$\left(301/100\right)\sqrt t$. The inequality
\[
 \frac7{11}t-\frac{301}{100}\sqrt t
 \ge-\frac{\left(301/100\right)^2}{4\left(7/11\right)}
 =-\frac{996611}{280000}
\]
is obtained by completing a square in $\sqrt t$.
Using it in \eqref{eq:allratioestimate} yields
\[
 N_A\left(t^2\right)-\frac{R^2-1}{4}t^2
 >\frac9{50}U-\frac34U^{1/3}-\frac{119}{24}
       -\frac{996611}{280000}.
\]
At $U=80$ this is greater than $315881/120000>0$, using
$80^{1/3}<13/3$; the right-hand side increases afterwards.

If $1/2\le\rho\le4/5$, then $t\ge U/2\ge40$, and the
curvature term is less than $4\sqrt t$, since
$\pi/\left(1-\rho\right)\le5\pi<16$.
The function $\left(7/11\right)t-\left(9/2\right)\sqrt t$ increases on $t\ge40$.
Consequently the excess is greater than
\[
 \left(\frac9{50}+\frac7{22}\right)U
 -\frac92\sqrt{U/2}-\frac34U^{1/3}-\frac{119}{24}.
\]
At $U=80$, use $\sqrt{40}<19/3$ and $80^{1/3}<13/3$
to bound this from below by $4153/1320>0$.
After division by $U$, every subtracted term decreases with $U$.

It remains to consider $t<2$. Write
$B_s=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\left|x\right|<s\right\}$, so $B=B_1$ is the unit disk
and $A=B_R\setminus\overline{B_1}$. Let $N_{B_s}\left(\Lambda\right)$
denote its Neumann count at energy $\Lambda$, and put
$\mathcal N_B\left(Z\right)=N_{B_1}\left(Z^2\right)$. Both conventions include zero.

Restricting a function in $H^1\left(B_R\right)$ to the two pieces gives an
inclusion into $H^1\left(B_1\right)\oplus H^1\left(A\right)$. The direct sum consists
of pairs of functions on the two pieces; unlike restrictions of
a single $H^1\left(B_R\right)$ function, their boundary values (traces) at the cutting circle
need not agree. Thus cutting and imposing independent Neumann
conditions enlarges the form domain, while the norm and energy
remain the sums of their values on the two pieces. The min--max
principle \cite{Davies} lowers the eigenvalues of the separated
problem. Its spectrum is the union of the two piece spectra,
with multiplicities, so
\[
 N_{B_R}\left(t^2\right)\le N_{B_1}\left(t^2\right)+N_A\left(t^2\right).
\]
The direction of the count inequality is opposite to that of the
eigenvalue inequality: lower eigenvalues give more modes below
the same threshold. Finally the substitution $x=Ry$ gives
$\mu_j\left(B_R\right)=R^{-2}\mu_j\left(B_1\right)$, and therefore
\[
 N_{B_R}\left(t^2\right)=\mathcal N_B\left(Rt\right)=\mathcal N_B\left(U\right),
 \qquad N_{B_1}\left(t^2\right)=\mathcal N_B\left(t\right).
\]
Rearranging the count comparison proves
\begin{equation}\label{eq:diskbracketinginner}
 N_A\left(t^2\right)\ge\mathcal N_B\left(U\right)-\mathcal N_B\left(t\right).
\end{equation}
No extra zero-mode correction is needed: the counts on both
pieces and the original disk all include their zero modes.
The inner count is at most three: angular orders at least two are
absent, and radial Dirichlet--Neumann interlacing leaves at most one
level in each of orders zero and one. Here $j_{m,1}$ denotes the
first positive zero of $J_m$; $j_{0,1}>2$, as follows from the
alternating series for $J_0$, and these zeros increase with order
\cite[Section~10.21]{NIST}.
Theorem~2.3 of \cite{FLPSballs} bounds the disk spectral count
below by its weighted lattice count. Proposition~6.5 of that paper
then bounds the latter count. Together they imply, for $U\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:diskFLPSremainder}
 \mathcal N_B\left(U\right)>
 \frac{U^2}{4}+\frac14\left[
  3G_U^{-1}\left(\frac14\right)
  -\left(1+\frac4\pi\right)U-3\right].
\end{equation}
Here $G_U$ is the disk action in Section~2.4, and
$G_U^{-1}\left(1/4\right)$ is its unique angular argument at height $1/4$.
The quarter-height tail estimate in Lemma~\ref{lem:outerfloors} gives
\[
 U-G_U^{-1}\left(\frac14\right)
 \le\left(\frac{9\pi^2}{128}\right)^{1/3}U^{1/3}<U^{1/3}.
\]
Substitution in \eqref{eq:diskFLPSremainder}, followed by $\pi>3$, yields
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal N_B\left(U\right)
 &>\frac{U^2}{4}+\left(\frac12-\frac1\pi\right)U
       -\frac34U^{1/3}-\frac34\\
 &>\frac{U^2}{4}+\frac U6-\frac34U^{1/3}-\frac34.
\end{align*}
Thus the annular excess is greater than
$F\left(U\right)=U/6-\left(3/4\right)U^{1/3}-15/4$. Since $80^{1/3}<5$,
$F\left(80\right)>35/6$, and
\[
 F'\left(U\right)=\frac16-\frac{1}{4U^{2/3}}>0\qquad\left(U\ge80\right).
\]
This proves the required positivity throughout the remaining range.
Scaling proves the theorem.

For every $0<\rho\le1/100$ and every $X\ge0$,

label: eq:diskcutN
title: Proof
body_md:
Apply the Neumann splitting argument of
\eqref{eq:diskbracketinginner} to the unit disk, now cutting at
radius $\rho$. The enlarged form domain is
$H^1\left(B_\rho\right)\oplus H^1\left(A_\rho\right)$, and the inner disk count at
energy $X^2$ is $\mathcal N_B\left(\rho X\right)$ by scaling.
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:diskcutN}
 \mathcal N_B\left(X\right)\le N_\rho\left(X^2\right)+\mathcal N_B\left(\rho X\right),\,\,\,
 N_\rho\left(X^2\right)\ge \mathcal N_B\left(X\right)-\mathcal N_B\left(\rho X\right).
\end{equation}
Let $n_m^{\mathrm N}\left(Y\right)$ and
$n_m^{\mathrm D}\left(Y\right)$ be the radial Neumann and Dirichlet
counts at energy $Y^2$ in angular order $m$. For $m\ge1$, the
interlacing $j'_{m,k}<j_{m,k}<j'_{m,k+1}$ implies
$n_m^{\mathrm N}\le n_m^{\mathrm D}+1$
\cite[Section~10.21(i)]{NIST}. Indeed, if $n$ derivative zeros
are at most $Y$, then, for $n\ge2$, the $n-1$ ordinary zeros
preceding the second through $n$th derivative zeros are also at most
$Y$. For $n\le1$ the inequality is immediate. The same argument
applies to $m=0$ with the convention $j'_{0,1}=0$, so its extra
mode includes the Neumann zero eigenvalue.

If $m>Y$, then $j'_{m,1}>m>Y$, and this order contributes no
Neumann mode. There are therefore at most $\left\lfloor Y\right\rfloor$
positive orders to retain. Order zero has angular multiplicity one,
and each positive order has multiplicity two. Summing the radial
inequalities gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathcal N_B\left(Y\right)
 &=n_0^{\mathrm N}\left(Y\right)
   +2\sum_{m=1}^{\left\lfloor Y\right\rfloor}n_m^{\mathrm N}\left(Y\right)\\
 &\le n_0^{\mathrm D}\left(Y\right)
   +2\sum_{m=1}^{\left\lfloor Y\right\rfloor}n_m^{\mathrm D}\left(Y\right)
   +1+2\left\lfloor Y\right\rfloor\\
 &\le\mathcal N_B^{\mathrm D}\left(Y\right)+2\left\lfloor Y\right\rfloor+1.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Theorem~1.2 of \cite{FLPSballs}, with $d=2$, states
$\mathcal N_B^{\mathrm D}\left(Y\right)<Y^2/4$ for $Y>0$.
At $Y=0$ the Dirichlet count is zero and the Neumann count is one.
Hence, for every $Y\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:diskcrudeupper}
 \mathcal N_B\left(Y\right)\le\frac{Y^2}{4}+2Y+1.
\end{equation}
Also, $\mathcal N_B\left(Y\right)=1$ for $0\le Y\le1$: for $m\ge1$ the first positive
zero of $J_m'$ is greater than $m$, and for $m=0$ the first
positive derivative zero is the first zero of $J_1$, greater than
one.

For the lower count, we use the choice
$\sigma=\arccos\left(5/6\right)$ from the proof of
\cite[Proposition~6.6]{FLPSballs}. At the angular argument
$x=X\cos\sigma$ the disk action has the value
\[
 G_X\left(X\cos\sigma\right)
 =\frac X\pi\left(\sin\sigma-\sigma\cos\sigma\right).
\]
Thus $G_X\left(5X/6\right)\ge1/4$ when
\[
 X\ge r_1\left(\sigma\right)
 :=\frac{\pi}{4\left(\sin\sigma-\sigma\cos\sigma\right)}
 =\frac{3\pi}{2\left(\sqrt{11}-5\sigma\right)}.
\]
Because $G_X$ is strictly decreasing, this is equivalent to
$G_X^{-1}\left(1/4\right)\ge5X/6$; it is the inverse-action
comparison of \cite[Lemma~4.8]{FLPSballs}.
To verify that $14$ suffices, the alternating cosine expansion gives
$\cos\left(59/100\right)\le1994397361/2400000000<5/6$,
so $\sigma<59/100$. Together with $\sqrt{11}>331/100$ and $\pi<22/7$,
this yields
\[
 r_1\left(\sigma\right)
 <\frac{33/7}{331/100-5\cdot59/100}=\frac{275}{21}<14.
\]
Substituting the inverse lower bound into
\eqref{eq:diskFLPSremainder} now gives, for $X\ge14$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathcal N_B\left(X\right)
 &>\frac{X^2}{4}+\frac14\left[
    3\cdot\frac56X-\left(1+\frac4\pi\right)X-3\right]\\
 &=\frac{X^2}{4}+\left(\frac38-\frac1\pi\right)X-\frac34.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:diskquantlower}
 \mathcal N_B\left(X\right)>\frac{X^2}{4}+aX-\frac34\quad\left(X\ge14\right),\qquad
 a=\frac{3\pi-8}{8\pi}>\frac{11}{200}.
\end{equation}
The rational coefficient bound follows from $\pi>25/8$:
$a=3/8-1/\pi>3/8-8/25=11/200$. The value $14$ is a sufficient
threshold for this parameter choice, not an optimal one.
The thresholds $32$ and $64$ are selected to give simple positive
rational margins in the two estimates: the first uses that the
removed disk has only one mode, while the second uses its crude
upper count. If $32\le X\le64$, then $\rho X<1$, so
\eqref{eq:diskcutN} and \eqref{eq:diskquantlower} yield
\[
 N_\rho\left(X^2\right)>\frac{X^2}{4}+aX-\frac74
 >\frac{X^2}{4}+\frac1{100}.
\]
Indeed $aX-7/4>\left(11/200\right)\cdot32-7/4=1/100$.
If $X\ge64$, use \eqref{eq:diskcrudeupper} as well to obtain
\[
 N_\rho\left(X^2\right)>
 \frac{1-\rho^2}{4}X^2+\left(a-2\rho\right)X-\frac74
 >\frac{1-\rho^2}{4}X^2+\frac{49}{100}.
\]
Here $a-2\rho>11/200-2/100=7/200$, and
$\left(7/200\right)\cdot64-7/4=49/100$.
Both high-frequency estimates are uniform in $0<\rho\le1/100$.

For $32\le X^2\le1024$ one still has $\mathcal N_B\left(\rho X\right)=1$.
Combining \eqref{eq:diskcutN} with the surplus in
Lemma~\ref{lem:diskanalyt_surplus} gives
$N_\rho\left(X^2\right)\ge X^2/4>\left(1-\rho^2\right)X^2/4$.

It remains to treat $X^2\le32$. In this range
$\left(1-\rho^2\right)X^2\le32$, so Proposition~\ref{prop:analyticfirsteight},
proved independently in Appendix~\ref{sec:analyticfirsteight}, gives
the required strict inequality. This includes $X=0$ by the zero mode.
All frequencies are now covered.

label: eq:rrrecurrence
title: Proof
body_md:
Set $\epsilon=10^{-5}$. On a radius cell $\left[a,b\right]$, the zero mode
first covers the energy interval
$\left[0,U_0\right]$, where $U_0=4/\left(1-a^2\right)-\epsilon$.
For a row starting at $L=U_{j-1}$, compute \eqref{eq:rrcount}
from \eqref{eq:rrmass}--\eqref{eq:rrenergy} and put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rrrecurrence}
 U_j=\min\left\{\frac{4c}{1-a^2}-\epsilon,100\right\}.
\end{equation}
The small positive rational offset $\epsilon$ turns the natural
Weyl endpoint $4c/\left(1-a^2\right)$ into a strict comparison. Its particular
size has no spectral meaning: the calculation checks that it is
small enough for every interval to advance to the next one.
Radius cells are obtained by starting from $\left[1/100,4/5\right]$ and
bisecting a cell whenever this recurrence fails to reach energy
$100$. Thus the rational radius endpoints in the table are determined
by a reproducible success criterion. The cutoff $100=10^2$ overlaps
the phase calculation, which begins at frequency $8$.
Only orders $m\le\left\lfloor\sqrt L\right\rfloor$ are used. Omitting any
other angular orders only decreases a lower counting bound.
The exact inertia computations give the following successive values
of $c$, including the initial count $1$ for the zero-mode interval:

 1/100&83/400&1,3,5,8,12,16,18,21,25\\
 83/400&81/200&1,3,5,7,9,12,14,18,22,24\\
 81/200&403/800&1,3,5,7,9,12,18,22\\

 241/400&561/800&1,3,7,11,13,15,17\\

name: Two endpoint radii

title: Proof
body_md:
By the exact phase identity in Lemma~\ref{lem:exactphasecount},
after rescaling the two arguments,
\[
 n_m\left(\rho,u\right)=
 \left\lfloor\frac{\varphi_m\left(u\right)-\varphi_m\left(\rho u\right)}{\pi}
 \right\rfloor+1.
\]
The branch convention is the same as in that lemma, including the
zero eigenvalue when $m=0$. By \eqref{eq:phasevelocity},
$\varphi_m$ decreases up to $s=m$ and increases thereafter;
when $m=0$ it is increasing throughout.  Its maximum on $\left[au,bu\right]$
therefore occurs at an endpoint.  Taking the floor in the exact
identity proves the assertion at frequency $u$.  Radial counting
functions are nondecreasing in the frequency, proving it for
$X\ge u$.  Summing with angular multiplicities gives
\eqref{eq:boxcount}; the omitted higher orders have nonnegative
counts. The endpoint selected by the minimum may depend on $m$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:certendpointcounts}
The quantities in \eqref{eq:certoutercount} and
\eqref{eq:certcorecount} are lower bounds for $n_m\left(\rho,u\right)$.
They remain valid when every action in a positive position is
replaced by a certified lower endpoint, every subtracted action
or phase error by a certified upper endpoint, and the floors are
then evaluated with integer arithmetic.

title: Proof
body_md:
When $m=u$, the outer bound is zero and is immediate. For $m<u$,
the outer bound follows from $\varphi_m\left(y\right)\le\pi/2$ for $y<m$
and the lower phase bound \eqref{eq:phaseinput}.  The core bound
uses the same lower bound at $u$, and the upper phase bound at $y$.
For $m=0$ its error is precisely bounded by $3/\left(8y\right)$ before division
by $\pi$.

For $m\ge1$, Lemma~\ref{lem:globalphaseerror} gives
$e_m\left(y\right)/\pi<1/2$ for every $y\ge m$, including the turning
endpoint. The other upper error is $E_m\left(y\right)/\pi$, so their minimum
is still an upper bound. For $m=0$ the explicit formula
$E_0\left(y\right)/\pi=3/\left(8\pi y\right)$ applies for every $y>0$; the global
$1/2$ cap is unnecessary and is not used.

All counts are nonnegative, and $n_0\left(\rho,u\right)\ge1$ because zero is
an eigenvalue.  These facts justify the maximum in
\eqref{eq:certcorecount}.  Finally, the floor function is
nondecreasing, so outward enclosures in the indicated directions
preserve each lower bound.

label: eq:certboxaccept
title: Proof
body_md:
The companion certificate contains 4,104 rectangles
$\left[a,b\right]\times\left[u,v\right]$ with rational endpoints.  For each rectangle
the interval evaluator supplies endpoint lower counts and
the integer
\[
 \mathcal L\left(a,b,u\right)=
 \min\left\{L_0\left(a,u\right),L_0\left(b,u\right)\right\}
 +2\sum_{m=1}^{\left\lfloor u\right\rfloor}
       \min\left\{L_m\left(a,u\right),L_m\left(b,u\right)\right\}.
\]
It verifies the strict rational inequality
\begin{equation}\label{eq:certboxaccept}
 4\mathcal L\left(a,b,u\right)>\left(1-a^2\right)v^2.
\end{equation}

\ref{lem:certendpointcounts} then prove the desired assertion
at every point of this closed rectangle, since
$\left(1-\rho^2\right)X^2\le\left(1-a^2\right)v^2$ there.

A separate
verification mode recomputes every endpoint lower count and every
inequality \eqref{eq:certboxaccept}.  It also checks the exact total
area and performs a rational vertical sweep: between consecutive
distinct radius endpoints, the active frequency intervals partition
$\left[8,80\right]$ with no gaps or overlapping interiors.  The first and last
radius endpoints are $1/100$ and $4/5$.  As all rectangles are closed,
their boundaries are included as well.  This proves that their union
is the whole required parameter rectangle, completing the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Scale the outer radius to one and put $\rho=r/R$ and
$X=R\sqrt\Lambda$. If $\rho\ge4/5$, then
$\left(R-r\right)/r\le1/4$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:thinall} applies.
If $0<\rho\le1/100$, use Theorem~\ref{thm:smallholeall}.
It remains to consider $1/100\le\rho\le4/5$.
For $0\le X\le10$, Lemma~\ref{lem:rrlowmiddle} applies;
for $8\le X\le80$, use Proposition~\ref{prop:compactbridge};
for $X\ge80$, use Theorem~\ref{thm:outereighty}.
The ratio $4/5$ is exactly the translation of
$\left(R-r\right)/r\le1/4$ into outer-radius normalization. The intervals
$\left[0,10\right]$ and $\left[8,80\right]$ overlap on $\left[8,10\right]$; the overlap gives
room for the distinct low-frequency and phase estimates to meet.
The threshold $80$ is included in both the compact and analytic
bounds. All ranges are closed and cover every $X\ge0$. This proves
\eqref{eq:allannulicount} for every pair of positive radii with
$r<R$. At $\Lambda=4k/\left(R^2-r^2\right)$, its right-hand side is $k$.
Thus there are at least $k+1$ eigenvalues, including zero, below or
equal to this energy, proving \eqref{eq:allannulieigenvalue}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $A=A_{r,R}$ and let $\mu_j\left(\Omega\right)$, $j\ge0$, be the Neumann
eigenvalues of $\Omega$, including all zero eigenvalues if $\Omega$
has more than one component. The spectrum of a Cartesian product
consists of sums of the spectra of its factors. Thus, for $E>0$,
\[
 N_{A\times\Omega}\left(E\right)
 =\sum_{\mu_j\left(\Omega\right)\le E}N_A\left(E-\mu_j\left(\Omega\right)\right)
 >\frac{\left|A\right|}{4\pi}\sum_{j\ge0}\left(E-\mu_j\left(\Omega\right)\right)_+,
\]
The sum is the Riesz mean of order one defined in the introduction. The strict inequality follows term by term
from Theorem~\ref{thm:allannuli}; the sum is nonempty because of the
zero mode. Laptev's Neumann trace inequality
\cite[Theorem~3.1]{Laptev} gives
\[
 \sum_{j\ge0}\left(E-\mu_j\left(\Omega\right)\right)_+
 \ge \frac{\left|\Omega\right|}{\left(4\pi\right)^{d/2}\Gamma\left(2+d/2\right)}E^{1+d/2}.
\]
Here $\Gamma\left(z\right)=\int_0^{+\infty} t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,\mathrm d t$ for $z>0$
is the gamma function. Since
$\omega_{d+2}=\pi^{1+d/2}/\Gamma\left(2+d/2\right)$, the product of the
two coefficients is
$\omega_{d+2}\left|A\right|\,\left|\Omega\right|/\left(2\pi\right)^{d+2}$, the Weyl coefficient
in dimension $d+2$. The zero mode also gives strict counting at
$E=0$. At
\[
 E_k=4\pi^2\left(\frac{k}
 {\omega_{d+2}\left|A\right|\,\left|\Omega\right|}\right)^{2/\left(d+2\right)},
\]
the Weyl term equals $k$, so the strict counting estimate gives
at least $k+1$ eigenvalues at or below $E_k$, including zero.
This yields the corollary.

title: Proof
body_md:
The $q$ rotated copies of $S_q$ partition the annulus up to their
boundary seams. Allowing independent traces on these seams enlarges
the Neumann form domain. The min--max principle \cite{Davies}
therefore gives $N_A\left(E\right)\le qN_{S_q}\left(E\right)$. As $\left|A\right|=q\left|S_q\right|$,
Theorem~\ref{thm:allannuli} implies
\[
 qN_{S_q}\left(E\right)\ge N_A\left(E\right)>\frac{q\left|S_q\right|}{4\pi}E.
\]
Dividing by $q$ proves the counting assertion. At
$E=4qk/\left(R^2-r^2\right)$ it supplies at least $k+1$ eigenvalues,
including zero. This proves the eigenvalue assertion. The argument
is the Neumann tiling transfer in
\cite[Theorem~1.8 and Remark~1.9]{FLPSballs}.

label: lem:angularfirstmonotone
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:angularfirstmonotone}
Normalize the outer radius to one. For an integer $m\ge1$, let
$\beta_m\left(\rho\right)$ be the lowest eigenvalue of
\[
 -u''-s^{-1}u'+m^2s^{-2}u=\beta u,
 \,\,\, \rho<s<1,\,\,\, u'\left(\rho\right)=u'\left(1\right)=0.
\]
Then $\beta_m$ is strictly decreasing on $\left(0,1\right)$. In particular,
\[
 \beta_1\left(\rho\right)<\frac{112}{33},\quad
 \beta_2\left(\rho\right)<\frac{75}{8},\quad
 \beta_3\left(\rho\right)<\frac{552}{31},\quad
 \beta_4\left(\rho\right)<\frac{1120}{39}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $m\ge1$. The variational characterization of the lowest
eigenvalue for this regular separated boundary problem is
\cite{Davies}
\[
 \beta_m\left(\rho\right)
 =\min_{0\ne v\in H^1\left(\rho,1\right)}
 \frac{\displaystyle\int_\rho^1
       \left(s\left|v'\right|^2+\frac{m^2}{s}\left|v\right|^2\right)\,\mathrm d s}
      {\displaystyle\int_\rho^1s\left|v\right|^2\,\mathrm d s}.
\]
A minimizer may be chosen nonnegative, since replacing it by its
absolute value does not change this quotient. The differential
equation then makes it strictly positive on the closed interval:
an interior zero of a nonnegative solution would also have zero
derivative, and a zero at either endpoint is accompanied by the
Neumann condition. In both cases uniqueness for the initial-value
problem would force the solution to vanish identically. Moreover,
every solution satisfying the outer Neumann condition is determined
by its value at $s=1$, so the eigenspace is one-dimensional.
Choose the positive eigenfunction $u\left(s,\rho\right)$ normalized by
$u\left(1,\rho\right)=1$.

We first justify its differentiation with respect to $\rho$.
Let $U\left(s,\lambda\right)$ solve
\[
 -\left(sU_s\right)_s+\frac{m^2}{s}U=\lambda sU,
 \qquad U\left(1,\lambda\right)=1,\qquad
 U_s\left(1,\lambda\right)=0.
\]
Subscripts denote partial derivatives. On any compact interval with
$s>0$, this initial-value solution depends smoothly on $s$ and
$\lambda$. The eigenvalue equation is
$F\left(\rho,\lambda\right):=U_s\left(\rho,\lambda\right)=0$.
At an eigenvalue put $Z=\partial_\lambda U$. Differentiating the
equation for $U$ gives
\[
 -\left(sZ_s\right)_s+\frac{m^2}{s}Z
 =\lambda sZ+sU,\qquad Z\left(1\right)=Z_s\left(1\right)=0.
\]
Multiplying this equation by $U$, subtracting the equation for $U$
multiplied by $Z$, and integrating yields
\[
 \int_\rho^1sU^2\,\mathrm d s
 =\left[s\left(ZU_s-UZ_s\right)\right]_\rho^1
 =\rho U\left(\rho,\lambda\right)Z_s\left(\rho,\lambda\right).
\]
Thus, at $\lambda=\beta_m\left(\rho\right)$,
\[
 \partial_\lambda F\left(\rho,\beta_m\left(\rho\right)\right)
 =\frac{\displaystyle\int_\rho^1sU^2\,\mathrm d s}
        {\rho U\left(\rho,\beta_m\left(\rho\right)\right)}>0.
\]
The implicit-function theorem therefore gives a smooth local
eigenvalue branch and a smooth eigenfunction
$u\left(s,\rho\right)=U\left(s,\beta_m\left(\rho\right)\right)$.
This branch is the lowest eigenvalue: under the linear change
$s=\rho+\left(1-\rho\right)y$, the Rayleigh quotient is defined on
the fixed space $H^1\left(0,1\right)$, with positive coefficients
depending continuously on $\rho$. On compact subsets of
$0<\rho<1$, their relative changes are uniformly small, so the
minimum is continuous in $\rho$. It must consequently agree locally
with the isolated root just constructed. Since $\rho$ was arbitrary,
$\beta_m$ is differentiable throughout $\left(0,1\right)$.

For the derivative calculation, write $\beta=\beta_m\left(\rho\right)$,
$u=u\left(s,\rho\right)$, and
$\dot u=\partial_\rho u\left(s,\rho\right)$, where $s$ is held fixed.
Define the energy and mass
\[
 E\left(\rho\right)=\int_\rho^1
       \left(su_s^2+\frac{m^2}{s}u^2\right)\,\mathrm d s,
 \qquad
 M\left(\rho\right)=\int_\rho^1su^2\,\mathrm d s>0.
\]
The weak eigenvalue equation gives $E=\beta M$. Leibniz's rule,
including the moving lower endpoint and the dependence of $u$ on
$\rho$, gives
\begin{align*}
 E'\left(\rho\right)
 &=-\left(\rho u_s\left(\rho,\rho\right)^2
              +\frac{m^2}{\rho}u\left(\rho,\rho\right)^2\right)
   +2\int_\rho^1\left(su_s\dot u_s+\frac{m^2}{s}u\dot u\right)\,\mathrm d s,
 \\
 M'\left(\rho\right)
 &=-\rho u\left(\rho,\rho\right)^2
   +2\int_\rho^1su\dot u\,\mathrm d s.
\end{align*}
Here $u_s\left(\rho,\rho\right)=0$. The cross term in $E'$ is
computed by integration by parts:
\begin{align*}
 \int_\rho^1\left(su_s\dot u_s+\frac{m^2}{s}u\dot u\right)\,\mathrm d s
 &=\left[su_s\dot u\right]_\rho^1
   +\int_\rho^1\left(-\left(su_s\right)_s+\frac{m^2}{s}u\right)\dot u\,\mathrm d s
 \\
 &=\beta\int_\rho^1su\dot u\,\mathrm d s.
\end{align*}
The boundary term vanishes because the original eigenfunction has
$u_s=0$ at both endpoints. No boundary condition on $\dot u$ is
needed: it is an admissible test function for the Neumann weak
equation. In fact, differentiating the moving boundary condition
$u_s\left(\rho,\rho\right)=0$ gives
$\dot u_s\left(\rho,\rho\right)+u_{ss}\left(\rho,\rho\right)=0$,
so $\dot u$ generally does not satisfy a homogeneous Neumann
condition at the inner endpoint.

Differentiate $E=\beta M$ and substitute the preceding formulas.
The two integrals containing $u\dot u$ cancel exactly, leaving
\[
 \beta_m'\left(\rho\right)M\left(\rho\right)
 =E'\left(\rho\right)-\beta M'\left(\rho\right)
 =\rho\left(\beta-\frac{m^2}{\rho^2}\right)
       u\left(\rho,\rho\right)^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \beta_m'\left(\rho\right)
 =\frac{\rho\left(\beta_m\left(\rho\right)-m^2/\rho^2\right)
             u\left(\rho,\rho\right)^2}
        {\displaystyle\int_\rho^1su\left(s,\rho\right)^2\,\mathrm d s}.
\]

To determine its sign, use the constant trial function $v=1$.
Its energy is $m^2\log\left(1/\rho\right)$ and its mass is
$\left(1-\rho^2\right)/2$. Hence
\[
 \beta_m\left(\rho\right)
 \le\frac{2m^2\log\left(1/\rho\right)}{1-\rho^2}
 =\frac{m^2\log\left(\rho^{-2}\right)}{1-\rho^2}
 <\frac{m^2\left(\rho^{-2}-1\right)}{1-\rho^2}
 =\frac{m^2}{\rho^2}.
\]
The strict inequality uses $\log z<z-1$ for $z>1$, with
$z=\rho^{-2}$. Since $\rho>0$, $u\left(\rho,\rho\right)>0$, and
$M\left(\rho\right)>0$, the derivative formula now gives
$\beta_m'\left(\rho\right)<0$ at every $0<\rho<1$.
Thus $\beta_m$ is strictly decreasing on the whole interval.
The assumption $m\ge1$ is essential for strictness; in order zero,
the constant eigenfunction gives $\beta_0\equiv0$.

For the explicit constants use
\[
 f_m\left(s\right)=s^m\left(1-a_ms^2\right),\qquad
 \left(a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4\right)=\left(1/3,1/2,2/3,2/3\right).
\]
The factor $s^m$ ensures regularity at the disk centre. The quadratic
correction reduces the energy of the pure monomial. These rational
coefficients give bounds sufficient for the first-eight-eigenvalue
estimate below; no optimality is claimed. Direct integration on the
unit disk, with the common angular factor suppressed, gives
\[
 K_m=\int_0^1\left(f_m'^2+m^2s^{-2}f_m^2\right)s\,\mathrm d s,
 \qquad M_m=\int_0^1f_m^2s\,\mathrm d s,
\]
Since
$f_m'\left(s\right)=ms^{m-1}-a_m\left(m+2\right)s^{m+1}$, expansion and integration
of the monomials give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 K_m
 &=\int_0^1\left(2m^2s^{2m-1}
     -4a_mm\left(m+1\right)s^{2m+1}
     +a_m^2\left(m^2+\left(m+2\right)^2\right)s^{2m+3}\right)\,\mathrm d s\\
 &=m-2a_mm+\frac{a_m^2\left(m^2+\left(m+2\right)^2\right)}{2m+4}
   =m\left(1-a_m\right)^2+\frac{2a_m^2}{m+2},\\
 M_m
 &=\int_0^1\left(s^{2m+1}-2a_ms^{2m+3}+a_m^2s^{2m+5}\right)\,\mathrm d s\\
 &=\frac1{2m+2}-\frac{a_m}{m+2}+\frac{a_m^2}{2m+6}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting the four rational coefficients gives the exact values
\[
 \begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
 m&a_m&K_m&M_m&K_m/M_m\\\hline
 1&1/3&14/27&11/72&112/33\\
 2&1/2&5/8&1/15&75/8\\
 3&2/3&23/45&31/1080&552/31\\
 4&2/3&16/27&13/630&1120/39
 \end{array}
\]
Fix $\rho>0$. Restricting $f_m$ to $\left[\varepsilon,1\right]$
gives a trial quotient tending to $K_m/M_m$ as
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$. For $0<\varepsilon<\rho/2$, monotonicity
and the variational bound give
$\beta_m\left(\rho/2\right)\le\beta_m\left(\varepsilon\right)
\le E_\varepsilon\left(f_m\right)/M_\varepsilon\left(f_m\right)$,
where $E_\varepsilon$ and $M_\varepsilon$ are the energy and mass
integrals over $\left[\varepsilon,1\right]$. Taking the limit and then
using strict monotonicity yields
\[
 \beta_m\left(\rho\right)<\beta_m\left(\rho/2\right)\le K_m/M_m.
\]
No numerical information about Bessel zeros is used.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:analyticfirsteight}
For every $0<r<R$, with $D=R^2-r^2$ and $\nu_0=0$,
\[
 \nu_k\left(A_{r,R}\right)<\frac{4k}{D}\,\,\,\left(1\le k\le8\right).
\]
In particular, the counting assertion needed here is
\[
 N_A\left(\Lambda\right)>\frac{D\Lambda}{4}
 \,\,\,\text{if }0\le D\Lambda\le32.
\]

title: Proof
body_md:
Scale to $R=1$, put $\rho=r$ and $D=1-\rho^2$.
Each nonzero angular order supplies two real modes, and distinct
orders are orthogonal for both the energy and mass forms.
Lemma~\ref{lem:angularfirstmonotone}, together with the zero mode, gives
\[
 \nu_2<\frac{112}{33}<4,\,\,\,
 \nu_4<\frac{75}{8}<12,\,\,\,
 \nu_6<\frac{552}{31}<20,\,\,\,
 \nu_8<\frac{1120}{39}<32.
\]
Since $D<1$, these prove the required bounds for $k=1,2,3,4,5,6,8$.

Only the seventh index needs an additional argument: the fourth
angular estimate alone is slightly larger than its Weyl threshold $28$.
The split at $\rho=1/5$ makes both the area reduction and the radial
trial-function estimate below sufficient. This split is convenient rather
than optimal. First suppose $\rho\ge1/5$. The fourth angular order gives
\[
 D\nu_7<D\frac{1120}{39}
 \le\frac{24}{25}\frac{1120}{39}<28.
\]
If $0<\rho\le1/5$, use the radial polynomial
$p\left(s\right)=1-3s^2+\tfrac32s^4$, subtracting its weighted mean on
$\left[\rho,1\right]$. Its full-disk weighted mean is zero, its mass is $1/10$,
and its energy is $3/2$. To quantify the mean subtraction, put
\[
 W_\rho=\int_\rho^1s\,\,\mathrm d s=\frac{1-\rho^2}{2},\,\,\,
 b_\rho=\int_\rho^1p\left(s\right)s\,\,\mathrm d s
        =-\int_0^\rho p\left(s\right)s\,\,\mathrm d s.
\]
The mean-zero trial function is $p-b_\rho/W_\rho$, with squared
weighted norm $\int_\rho^1p^2s\,\,\mathrm d s-b_\rho^2/W_\rho$.
Since $\left|p\right|\le1$ on $\left[0,\rho\right]$, the lost disk mass is at most
$\rho^2/2$, and $\left|b_\rho\right|\le\rho^2/2$. Its norm is therefore
at least
\[
 \frac1{10}-\frac{\rho^2}{2\left(1-\rho^2\right)}
 \ge\frac1{10}-\frac1{48}=\frac{19}{240}.
\]
Its Rayleigh quotient is therefore at most $360/19<20$.
Together with the constant and the first three nonzero angular
orders this gives an eight-dimensional trial space whose maximal
quotient is less than $20$. Hence $D\nu_7<20<28$ also in this case.

For the counting statement set $q=D\Lambda$. If $0\le q<4$, the
zero mode suffices. Otherwise $k=\left\lfloor q/4\right\rfloor$ lies between
one and eight, and $\nu_k<4k/D\le\Lambda$. Thus
$N_A\left(\Lambda\right)\ge k+1>q/4$, including $q=32$.
